subject: suprisingly bad fit indices compared to same model in lavaan + information curves for bifactor model

messages.author: 5dadf4dbf792b603
messages.subject: suprisingly bad fit indices compared to same model in lavaan + information curves for bifactor model
parts:
Dear all,

I am a new MIRT user. So, maybe I made a rookie mistake. Any advice is much appreciated.

The standardized loadings were pretty much as expected but I don't understand why the fit indices are so bad.
> M2(NARQf)
            M2   df p     RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95       TLI       CFI     SRMSR
stats 29323.39 1605 0 0.0964363 0.09544579 0.09737816 0.2378464 0.2536568 0.1414085

In lavaan with the categorical data option, I got for the same model a CFI of .988 and a TLI of .985, the RMSEA was 0.057. (N= 1858)

Here is the code I used (It's a code for two bifactor models and the general factors are correlated):

NARQm <- '
f1 = 1,2,8
f2 = 7,16,18
f3 = 4,11,12
f4 = 6,9,10
f5 = 13,14,17
ADM = 1,2,8,7,16,18,3,5,15
RIV = 4,11,12,6,9,10,13,14,17
COV = ADM*RIV'

modelNARQ <- mirt.model(NARQm)

NARQf <- mirt(data=Data, model=modelNARQ, itemtype='graded')

Any idea what could have went wrong?

An additional question would be: I would like to calculate information curves for the two general factors (ADM + RIV). However, I get the following error:
> plot(NARQf)
Error in .local(x, y, ...) : Can't plot high dimensional solutions.

Does anybody have an idea how I could plot the information curves for ADM and RIV based on this model?

cheers,
Michael

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: suprisingly bad fit indices compared to same model in lavaan + information curves for bifactor model
parts:
Hi Michael,

You definitely want to use the bfactor() function instead of mirt() here. mirt() uses a grid of quadrature for integration, and with the five factors defined here the quadpts are set equal to 3 (very bad and quite inaccurate). bfactor() uses a dimensional reduction algorithm to more accurately estimate the model, and in your case you'll want to build a two-tier model. This will also improve the accuracy of the M2 statistic (since dimensional reduction methods will be used there as well). 

Onto the second part, beyond 2 dimensions (or 3 if slices are made at each level of the third factor....which I think may be supported in the plot generic) graphics can not be drawn since they are hyper-dimensional. itemplot() can work if you pass a drop.zeros = TRUE option, but for the full test information a plot is not possible. Cheers.

Phil

best,

On Thu, Aug 28, 2014 at 8:28 AM, Michael Paul Grosz <michael.p...@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear Phil,

Thank you very much for your adivce!
I made now use of the bfactor() function and fitted a two-tier model (good to know that this is the name of the model that I fitted).
The model fit improved considerably but it is still significantly lower than the fit of the equivalent model in lavaan.
> M2(NARQtier)
            M2 df p      RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95       TLI       CFI     SRMSR
stats 713.0453 47 0 0.08735686 0.08173241 0.09305558 0.7628403 0.8623888 0.1588775
 
Do you have any idea why the fit is lower than in lavaan?

I imagine the M2 functions slightly differently than the standard SEM fit measures, especially since it is explicitly for categorical data (rather than a two-stage/weighted approximation in SEM). Though it's hard to say. Another possibility is to increase the quadpts to see if improving the numerical integration affects the model, though if you used the default of 21 then I doubt increasing further will make that much difference.
Do you know a way how I could improve the fit?

One thing you can and should do when the M2* doesn't fit well is inspect the observed covariance residuals by passing M2(..., residmat = TRUE). Larger residuals can indicate that covariation still exists between variables and should be fixed (in the same spirit as interpreting the residual covariance matrix in SEM and factor analysis).
or are these fit indices normal for full-information item FA models with such a complexity?

This is the harder question, since relatively little is known about IRT fit statistics. It's possible they don't behave exactly the same as SEM measures, but since so little research has been performed with them it's difficult to say. Hope that helps.

Phil

best,
Michael

messages.subject: Re: suprisingly bad fit indices compared to same model in lavaan + information curves for bifactor model
parts:
I find it to be much more of a blessing than a curse. The so-called "established" fit statistic cutoffs (which were all exclusively established for continuous variable models by the way....so the results you obtain from the WLSMV estimator in lavaan for categorical data likely are not what you think) are far too cookie-cutter for real data analysis. Fit measures are just tools to help understand different aspects of estimated models, and don't somehow represent a type of verisimilitude with the empirical world. I think every article proposing fit measures in SEM have emphasized this, so if anything regarding IRT fit measures we hopefully can learn not fall into the same pattern of mistakes that were made in SEM. At least, I certainly hope fit in IRT doesn't go down that path; time will tell.....Cheers.

Phil

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: suprisingly bad fit indices compared to same model in lavaan + information curves for bifactor model
parts:
For model selection information statistics are still good candidates for the job, and the fit indices given in M2() are fine to use just so long as they don't carry the popular SEM definitions. E.g., a value of CFI = .85 shouldn't automatically be interpreted as an 'okay' fit, but rather that could be quite good for a categorical model, and may be an improvement over other competing models that were tested in this and other datasets. Interpret these stats for what they mean (i.e., the CFI measures how much worse a model fits, in terms of the chi-squared value, when only the intercept parameters are modeled relative to the parameters that were fit to the data....that could be useful to know, but then again it also seems rather ambiguous when you actually say it out loud).

If I had to place bets, I would probably say that the SRMR statistic and the associated residuals (as well as other item fit statistics) are more important than any global stat since they have very clear meanings globally and locally. That's not to say that they are the best, just that they are easier to interpret and fairly helpful with item analysis. IMO, it's much more important to know if particular areas of the model are functioning well rather than if the model globally fits the data exactly (which is a very difficult, and in many way a trially impossible task since statistical models are only approximations to the world anyway). Cheers.

Phil

Phil
